meta.title: Who really said "Nature gives you the face you have at twenty; it is up to you to merit the face you have at fifty"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Coco Chanel published a version — but the real 1938 Paris Vogue maxim has three parts, not two. What the popular English wording leaves out.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Nature gives you the face you have at twenty; it is up to you to merit the face you have at fifty'?
meta.ogDescription: Chanel's maxim appeared in Paris Vogue, September 1938 — in three clauses. The famous two-part English line is a later condensation.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1883–1971 · French couturière, founder of the House of Chanel
answer.sourceLine: Chanel really did publish a maxim of this kind: Quote Investigator ↗ documents it in a set of “Maximes et Sentences” credited to Gabrielle Chanel in the Paris Vogue of September 1938. But the French there has three limbs — twenty, thirty, fifty — and the two-part English line that circulates today drops the middle one. No published translation has been traced that carries this exact shortened wording, so the sentiment is Chanel’s while the sentence is a later condensation.

source.excerpt:
La nature vous donne votre visage de vingt ans; la vie modèle votre visage de trente; mais celui de cinquante ans, c’est à vous de le mériter.

“Nature gives you the face you have at twenty; life molds the face you have at thirty; it is up to you to merit the face you have at fifty.”
trail: 1891 — The earliest evidence Quote Investigator finds for the idea is in L. E. Chittenden’s Recollections of President Lincoln and His Administration ↗, where Lincoln’s Secretary of War Edwin M. Stanton says a man of fifty is responsible for his face.

September 1938 — The Paris Vogue prints “Maximes et Sentences” credited to Gabrielle Chanel, including the three-part French maxim, per Quote Investigator ↗. Vogue’s French edition, founded in 1920 ↗, ran until the Occupation halted it in 1940.
March 1939 — The Toronto Globe and Mail carries an English variant citing the Paris periodical Les Annales — still with all three clauses, per Quote Investigator ↗.
Today — The two-part form dominates quote sites, while Wikiquote’s Chanel page ↗ does not carry the line at all.
source.excerptNote: French text and English rendering as printed by Quote Investigator ↗ from the September 1938 Paris Vogue. The middle clause is the part the famous English version drops.
source.rightsHolder: The estate of Gabrielle Chanel and the publisher of Vogue
source.rightsNote: The maxim was first published in Vogue (Paris) in September 1938 — well after the 1931 United States public-domain cutoff — so the text should be treated as in copyright, with rights resting with Chanel’s estate and/or the magazine’s publisher. The popular English condensation has no identified translator, which is a further reason not to assume it is free to reuse. Short quotation with attribution is normal practice; wholesale reproduction is not.

author.heading: Who was Coco Chanel?
author.metaLine: 1883–1971 · French couturière · founder of the House of Chanel
author.bio: Gabrielle Bonheur “Coco” Chanel was born in Saumur in 1883 and died in Paris in 1971. She rebuilt twentieth-century women’s dress around ease and simplicity — jersey, the collarless suit, the little black dress — and turned a milliner’s shop into a luxury house whose scent, Chanel No. 5, outlived her. She was also a practised aphorist: fashion magazines printed her sayings as copy in their own right, which is exactly how this line reached print.

misattribution.heading: What gets lost, and who else gets the credit
misattribution.intro: This is not a fake Chanel quote — it is a real Chanel maxim that has been trimmed, and a thought that predates her by decades in other mouths.

items.why: The French printed in the September 1938 Paris Vogue runs in three clauses: nature gives the face at twenty, life models the one at thirty, and only the face at fifty is yours to merit. The circulating English line silently deletes the thirty-year-old middle clause, as Quote Investigator ↗ shows by printing the original.

The earliest evidence Quote Investigator located for this family of remarks is L. E. Chittenden’s 1891 Recollections of President Lincoln and His Administration ↗, recounting Lincoln’s Secretary of War Edwin M. Stanton saying that a man of fifty is responsible for his face.

items.who: George Orwell, Albert Camus, Ingrid Bergman, Albert Schweitzer, Maurice Chevalier and others
items.why: Quote Investigator ↗ lists all of these among the people credited with one version or another of “the face you deserve.” The idea is a floating aphorism; Chanel’s contribution is one particular, datable phrasing of it.

misattribution.truthLine: Chanel earned this one — but in three parts, in French, in Vogue in September 1938. Quote it in full, or say plainly that you are quoting a shortened English rendering. See the evidence ↗

context.heading: Why the middle clause matters
lead: The full maxim is an argument in three moves, not two. Nature hands you a face at twenty; life shapes the one you have at thirty; and only the third — the face at fifty — is yours to earn. Drop the middle limb and you lose the hinge: the idea that experience does some of the work on a face before character gets its turn.

Chanel was a good subject for this sort of thing because magazines treated her talk as publishable copy. Quote Investigator ↗ also shows the thought was already in circulation in other forms decades before: its earliest evidence is an anecdote in L. E. Chittenden’s 1891 Recollections of President Lincoln and His Administration, in which Lincoln’s Secretary of War Edwin M. Stanton says that a man of fifty is responsible for his face.
detailsBody: The September 1938 Paris Vogue French text, as given by QI: “La nature vous donne votre visage de vingt ans; la vie modèle votre visage de trente; mais celui de cinquante ans, c’est à vous de le mériter.”

A variant reached English in March 1939, when the Toronto Globe and Mail printed it citing the Paris periodical Les Annales: nature gives you the face you have at twenty, life models the face you have at thirty, but the face you have at fifty is the one you deserve. That English form still has all three limbs.

QI lists the wider family of “the face you deserve” remarks as having been credited to Abraham Lincoln, Coco Chanel, George Orwell, Albert Camus, Ingrid Bergman, Albert Schweitzer, Maurice Chevalier, Edwin M. Stanton, William H. Seward, Edward Lee Hawk, and an unnamed U.S. senator.
context.pull: Nature gives the face; life shapes it; only the last one is earned.
